steps: Surds: find the largest square number factor and simplify
To rationalise: multiply numerator and denominator by the surd (or conjugate)
Bounds: half a unit above and below the rounded value
Max value of a/b: use upper a, lower b
pre_method_card.title: Indices, Surds & Bounds
pre_method_card.content:
Surds are irrational square roots left in exact form, e.g. \(\sqrt{2}\), \(\sqrt{5}\). They cannot be written as exact decimals.

Simplifying surds: Find the largest square factor: \(\sqrt{50} = \sqrt{25 \times 2} = 5\sqrt{2}\). To add/subtract surds, they must have the same root: \(3\sqrt{2} + 5\sqrt{2} = 8\sqrt{2}\).

Rationalising the denominator: Multiply top and bottom by the surd: \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\). For \(\frac{1}{a + \sqrt{b}}\), multiply by the conjugate \(a - \sqrt{b}\).

Error bounds: A measurement of \(x\) rounded to some degree of accuracy has bounds: \(\text{lower} \leq x < \text{upper}\). For \(5.3\) to 1 d.p.: \(5.25 \leq x < 5.35\). To maximise \(\frac{a}{b}\), use upper \(a\) and lower \(b\).

steps: Simplify a surd by pulling out the largest square factor
Rationalise: multiply by the surd, or by the conjugate for a two-term denominator
Bounds: half a unit above and below the rounded value
Largest value of a/b: use upper a and lower b
now_method_card.title: Indices, Surds & Bounds
now_method_card.content:
Surds are exact square roots such as \(\sqrt{2}\). Simplify by pulling out the largest square factor: \(\sqrt{50} = 5\sqrt{2}\). Add only like surds: \(2\sqrt{3} + 5\sqrt{3} = 7\sqrt{3}\).

Rationalise by multiplying top and bottom by the surd, or by the conjugate \(a - \sqrt{b}\) for a two-term denominator.

Bounds lie half a unit each side of a rounded value. To make \(\frac{a}{b}\) largest, use the upper bound of a and the lower bound of b.
